title: Fertility changes US mothers’ labor-force participation and remote-work patterns across the pre- and post-pandemic periods
source_unit: US mothers, fertility, labor-force participation, remote work, occupation teleworkability, child penalties, and period before/after 2020

observations.period: American Community Survey 2003–2024; pre-COVID and post-2020 comparisons

denominator.unit: US mothers in harmonized individual-level ACS data; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

labor_force_participation.unit: fertility significantly reduces mothers’ labor-force participation across the sample period

pre_2020_remote_work.unit: before the COVID-19 pandemic, an additional child increases the likelihood of working remotely

post_2020_remote_work.unit: after 2020, an additional child has a negative effect on remote work when remote work is common

occupation_selection.unit: patterns are not driven by changing selection into teleworkable occupations or observable characteristics of compliers

child_penalty.unit: remote work in its current form has limited potential to meaningfully reduce child penalties for higher-order births

observations.method: Causal fertility estimates use harmonized ACS data and exogenous variation from the sex composition of the first two children and twin births at the second parity.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, effect sizes, confidence intervals, exact remote-work definitions, or all exclusion assumptions. Remote work is not the same as job quality, flexibility, care time, household wellbeing, or equal access; the period shift may reflect broader changes in work and family institutions.
observations.subgroup: US mothers, with comparisons across fertility exposure and pre-2020 versus post-2020 remote-work conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Remote work may be less feasible or attractive for many women because of employer expectations, care intensity, housing, occupation, schedule, or job quality; labor-force participation changes do not alone identify voluntary choice, constraint, income, or wellbeing.

related_sources.claim: Persistent labor-force exit is concentrated among low-income and low-skill workers, with limited replacement of lost W-2 income.
Minimum-wage hours responses differ across immigrant and native workers, highlighting heterogeneous work control and labor-market position.
AI-skilled employment and organization capital are associated with recent firm productivity growth, without establishing worker control or household benefit.

boundary: This record adds a fertility, care, and remote-work arrangement layer to the US industrial/consumer program. It does not establish the size of income, care-time, housing, health, or wellbeing effects, or that remote work is uniformly available or beneficial to mothers.
